rulebook.setup: Remove the face cards. Ace is 1. Shuffle and deal twenty cards face down to each player.
rulebook.turns: Both players turn up two cards and add their values. Compare the two sums. The larger sum claims the four cards. A tie sets those cards aside until the next higher sum claims them.
rulebook.finish: After ten flips of two cards per player, count the claimed cards. The player with more wins. Unresolved tie cards stay aside.
rulebook.teach: Start with one pair at a time. Ask the player to say both numbers and show how they made the sum. Compare totals after both players have checked their work.

rulebook.setup: Remove the face cards. Ace is 1. Deal twenty face-down cards to each player.
rulebook.turns: Both players turn up two cards. Subtract the smaller rank from the larger. The larger difference claims all four cards. Set tied cards aside for the next higher difference.
rulebook.finish: Count claimed cards after ten flips of two cards each. The higher card count wins. Unresolved tie cards stay aside.
rulebook.teach: Say the answer and reverse-check it. If 9 − 6 = 3, then 6 + 3 = 9. Introduce signed differences as a distinct classroom variant.

rulebook.setup: Use Ace–10 with Ace worth 1. Lay nine cards face up in a three-by-three grid. Keep the rest as a stock.
rulebook.turns: Find two or three cards that total 10. Name the equation, collect them, and refill the empty spots from the stock. If there is no combination, end the round. The browser version scores one point per combination.
rulebook.finish: Count one point per valid combination. In group play, alternate turns or work together to beat a previous total.
rulebook.teach: Point to the first card and ask what still needs to be added. Show another way to reach 10 with different cards.

rulebook.setup: Use Ace–10 with Ace worth 1. Lay nine cards face up and leave the rest in a stock.
rulebook.turns: Select two or three cards totaling 15. Say the equation before collecting them. Fill empty spaces from the stock. Stop when no combination remains.
rulebook.finish: Award one point for each valid group. Take turns in group play or see how many combinations the table can find together.
rulebook.teach: Compare 7 + 8 and 4 + 5 + 6. Ask whether the order of the addends changes the total.

rulebook.setup: Take ranks Ace through 6 from two suits. Shuffle the twelve cards and arrange them face down.
rulebook.turns: Turn up two cards. If their ranks match, keep the pair. Otherwise turn both face down in their original positions. In multiplayer, pass after each attempt.
rulebook.finish: With one player, clear the grid and count the attempts. With several players, the most pairs wins.
rulebook.teach: Use row-and-column language to remember positions. Start with fewer pairs and use a card holder or a second person to help turn cards if needed.

title: Blackjack (21)
deck: Standard deck, one or more decks

rulebook.setup: The browser table uses one deck, one learner and a dealer, with no stakes. Give each two cards. The dealer shows one. Every number card has face value, each face card is 10, and an ace counts as 11 unless that would bust, then as 1.
rulebook.turns: A two-card 21 is a natural and settles the hand first. Otherwise, take another card or stand. A sum above 21 busts. Once you stand, the dealer reveals their other card and draws below 17. The dealer stands on every 17, including a soft 17.
rulebook.finish: Dealer bust gives any surviving hand the win. Otherwise compare totals at or below 21, with equal totals a tie. This teaching table uses hit and stand.
rulebook.teach: Compare A + 6 with A + 6 + 8. Explain why one ace changes its value. Estimate how many ranks could bust a hard 16, then check using the cards already seen.

sources.label: Hi-Lo rank values and true count

rulebook.setup: Shuffle a complete deck. Start at zero. Give ranks 2–6 a value of +1, 7–9 a value of 0, and tens, faces, and aces a value of −1.
rulebook.turns: Reveal one card at a time. Add its assigned value to the running count. At a checkpoint, divide the running count by the estimated number of decks remaining to get the true count.
rulebook.finish: A complete deck returns the running count to zero. Compare your count with the answer at several points rather than checking only the final zero.
rulebook.teach: Practice 3, king, 8, 6. The running totals are +1, 0, 0, +1. At a running count of +6 with three decks left, the true count is +2. This is a composition estimate. The exact next-card odds require tracking the rank or category itself.

rulebook.setup: Deal ten cards per player. Turn one card up beside the stock. Non-dealer gets first refusal of the upcard. If both decline, non-dealer draws from stock.
rulebook.turns: Draw the top stock or discard card, then discard one. An upcard taken this turn cannot immediately be returned. Keep sets of 3–4 equal ranks or same-suit runs of at least three, with ace low. Count unmatched cards at ace 1, faces 10, others face value. After discarding, knock at 10 or less. Zero is gin.
rulebook.finish: After an ordinary knock, the opponent can lay off on the knocker’s melds. If the knocker still has less deadwood, score the difference. Otherwise the opponent scores the difference plus 10. For gin there are no layoffs, and the winner scores 20 plus opponent deadwood. With two stock cards left and no knock, cancel the deal. Play to 100 before agreed bonuses.
rulebook.teach: Keep a private deadwood total and a public running score. Discuss what a taken discard suggests. The browser drill practices tallying and discarding, one hand at a time.

rulebook.setup: Deal ten each for two players, seven each for three or four, six each for five or six. Turn up one card beside the face-down stock.
rulebook.turns: Draw from the stock or the top discard. You may lay down same-rank sets or same-suit runs of at least three, or add cards to an existing meld. End by discarding, unless you have already used your last card. You cannot immediately discard the upcard you drew.
rulebook.finish: The first person out wins the hand. Score the cards remaining in opponents’ hands as ace 1, faces 10, other cards face value. Agree on the session target before play. Recycle the discard pile when the stock runs out according to the linked edition.
rulebook.teach: Lay out a same-rank set and a same-suit run side by side. Take turns checking whether a card fits either group.

title: 500 Rummy
deck: Standard deck with jokers, add a second pack for 5+

rulebook.setup: Use a 52-card deck and two jokers, or double for five or more. Deal thirteen to each if two play, seven each otherwise. Start one face-up discard.
rulebook.turns: Draw from stock or take a card from the spread discard pile. When reaching below its top, take all the cards above the chosen one and immediately meld the chosen card. Lay same-rank sets or same-suit runs of at least three, or add to melds. Discard to end a normal turn.
rulebook.finish: When someone empties their hand or the stock is exhausted when a draw is wanted, each player scores the value of their own melded cards minus what remains in hand. Use the linked edition for joker and ace points. Add each result to the running score, with highest score winning once the session threshold is crossed.
rulebook.teach: Make two columns, melded and remaining. Add each column, then subtract. Compare taking the top discard with reaching deeper and accepting extra cards.

title: Six-card Cribbage
deck: Standard 52-card deck and a cribbage board or score sheet

rulebook.setup: Deal six each. Both players choose two cards for the dealer’s crib. Cut a shared starter. If it is a jack, the dealer scores two.
rulebook.turns: Alternate playing cards and call the total without exceeding 31. Ace is 1 and faces are 10. Score 2 for 15 or 31, 2 for a pair, 6 for three of a kind, 12 for four, and length for a run. If neither can continue, score one for the last card unless it made 31, then reset the count. The other player leads the next sequence.
rulebook.finish: Count non-dealer hand, dealer hand, then crib, each with the starter. Score two per 15 or pair and length per run. A four-card hand flush scores 4, five with starter scores 5, and crib flush requires five. A jack of the starter suit in the hand or crib scores 1. First to 121 wins immediately.
rulebook.teach: Teach pegging and hand counting separately. Then exhibit how the same cards may participate in more than one scoring combination.

title: Trash (Garbage)
deck: One standard deck per two players

rulebook.setup: Lay ten face-down cards per player in two rows of five. The slots represent ace through ten. Leave the rest as the draw stock.
rulebook.turns: Draw one card from stock or the top discard. Put a numbered card in its numbered slot if that slot is unfilled or held a wild jack, then try to play the displaced card. A jack can fill any unfilled slot. A king, queen, or unusable number ends the turn and is discarded.
rulebook.finish: The browser version is a solo practice round. At the full table, after a player completes their layout, others get a final turn. Players completing their layout start the next round with one fewer slot. Win by completing a one-card layout.
rulebook.teach: Have the learner point out which position an ace, five, or ten belongs in before playing it.

title: Crazy Eights
deck: Standard 52-card deck, add a second for large tables

rulebook.setup: In this Academy two-player edition deal five cards each. Turn up a non-eight to start the discard pile. The browser uses an automated opponent.
rulebook.turns: Match the current rank or suit. An eight is wild and lets you name any suit. If you have no legal card, draw one and end the turn. When the stock is empty, recycle all discards except the top card. Pass if no draw is possible.
rulebook.finish: The first player with no cards wins the round. If both players pass with no supply, count remaining cards and award the round to the player with fewer, or call an equal count a draw.
rulebook.teach: Ask the learner to explain whether rank, suit, or the wild-card rule makes a play legal. Try keeping an eight until it is useful.

rulebook.setup: Shuffle a standard deck and divide it equally into two face-down piles. Rank ace high and two low.
rulebook.turns: Turn up one card each. The higher takes both under their own pile. In this short-war edition, a tie means both put one card down and one up. The higher face-up card takes the pot. Repeat on another tie.
rulebook.finish: The player who accumulates all the cards wins. Before play agree how to handle a player with too few cards to complete a war, or use a fixed number of rounds and count cards.
rulebook.teach: Compare ranks aloud and place a reference strip on the table for face cards.

rulebook.setup: Deal seven cards each for two or three players, five each for four or more. Keep the rest as a draw pile.
rulebook.turns: Ask a specific player for a rank you hold. They give all their cards of that rank if they have any. On success go again. Otherwise draw one. Go again if it is the requested rank, or pass. Lay down each four-of-a-kind book.
rulebook.finish: If you have no cards on your turn, take one from stock if available. When all books are made, the most books wins.
rulebook.teach: Model the full request once, then let learners remember who asked for each number. Use a face-up demonstration hand for the first turn.

rulebook.setup: Deal thirteen cards each. Pass three left, right, across, then hold, repeating that pattern each round.
rulebook.turns: Lead the two of clubs. Follow suit whenever possible. Highest of the led suit wins. First trick: keep penalty cards back if a legal non-penalty card is available. Hearts cannot be led until broken by a discard or the leader holds only hearts.
rulebook.finish: Score 1 per captured heart and 13 for the queen of spades. Taking all penalties assigns 26 to each opponent in this edition. At 100 or higher by any player, the lowest total wins.
rulebook.teach: Track the queen of spades and then count which spades are still out. Compare winning a trick with wanting to win it.

rulebook.setup: Deal thirteen each, with partners across. Each bids how many tricks they expect, and partners’ bids are added. This beginner edition omits nil bids.
rulebook.turns: Follow suit when possible. Highest spade wins any trick containing spades. Otherwise highest in the led suit wins. The winner leads next. Lead spades only after they have been played to another suit, or when you hold only spades.
rulebook.finish: Meeting the team bid earns ten points per bid trick plus a point per overtrick. Failing loses ten per bid trick. Every ten overtricks costs 100. Agree to a target, often 500.
rulebook.teach: Explain trump and follow-suit with an open four-card trick. Ask each team to record which spades have been played.

title: Scopa
deck: Italian 40-card pack, or English suits with 8–10 removed

rulebook.setup: Use a 40-card deck. Deal three to each and four face up to the table. With English suits use ace–7 and J/Q/K as 8/9/10, with diamonds replacing coins.
rulebook.turns: Play one card. Capture a single card of equal value if one exists. Otherwise capture a set that sums to it if possible. Without a capture, leave the card on the table. Re-deal three per player when hands are empty until stock runs out. Each sweep scores one except on the last play.
rulebook.finish: Give remaining table cards to the last capturer. Award one each for most cards, most coins, the seven of coins, and best primiera, plus sweeps. In primiera, select your highest-valued card per suit using the linked point table. A tied majority scores zero. Play to 11 or an agreed target.
rulebook.teach: With table cards 2, 3 and 5, show why a played 5 captures the single 5 before considering 2 + 3.

sources.label: David Parlett, history of patience games

rulebook.setup: Deal seven columns with one through seven cards, all face down except each column’s top card. Put the rest in the stock.
rulebook.turns: Build downward on the tableau in alternating colors. Move a legal ordered sequence as a unit, and reveal newly exposed face-down cards. Only a king or a sequence headed by a king fills an empty column. Build suit foundations upwards from ace to king. In this draw-one practice edition, turn stock cards one at a time to the waste and reuse the waste when needed.
rulebook.finish: Win when all four suit foundations reach king. If the position has no useful legal moves, stop or replay from the same deal.
rulebook.teach: Point to moves that uncover hidden cards. Compare two legal moves before choosing.

sources.label: Pagat Poker rules and hand ranks

rulebook.setup: Deal two private cards to each person. Reveal three shared cards, then a fourth and fifth. Before each reveal put one card aside face down.
rulebook.turns: Find the best five-card hand from your two private cards and the five shared cards. Use zero, one or two of your private cards. Compare practice hands as more public cards arrive.
rulebook.finish: From low to high: high card, pair, two pair, three of a kind, straight, flush, full house, four of a kind, straight flush. Use ranks of the matching group or highest cards, then unused cards in descending order to break ties. Identical five-card values tie.
rulebook.teach: Deal face up first so learners can explain which five cards they used. A classroom showdown uses score marks and no wagering.

title: Game of Leaves (yezi xi)

sources.label: Andrew Lo’s study in the Bulletin of SOAS

research: Early descriptions survive. The full rules and whether the historical pastime involved cards are unresolved. Compare historical terms, chronology and the alternative reading that it involved dice or promotion rules before designing a speculative teaching edition.
